definition.text: Natural resource management is the managing of land, water, soil, plants and animals with attention to how it affects life for people now and in the future.

facts.text: It deals with how people and natural landscapes interact, recognizing that livelihoods depend on healthy, productive land.
It brings together heritage protection, land-use planning, water management, biodiversity conservation and the future of farming, mining, tourism, fishing and forestry.
In the 20th century people saw that strict preservation had not stopped resources declining, so a more integrated approach took in social, economic and political sides.
Its issues are complex and contested: natural cycles are linked, and a change in one can have long-lasting, even irreversible, effects.
Managers must also weigh many stakeholders, policies, politics, borders and economic effects.
Tools such as GIS help by overlaying data sets, for example rainfall, cleared land and erosion, to plan bush regeneration.

definition.text: Resource management approaches can be grouped by who holds rights over a resource: the state, a private owner, a group, no one, or a mix.

facts.text: Under state property the state owns and controls the resource, and others use it only with permission, as in US national forests and parks.
Under private property a defined person or company owns the resource and bears both its benefits and its duties.
Common property is in effect the private property of a group, such as a community forest.
Open-access resources have no owner, anyone may use them, and they are the most exploited; a lake fishery is an example.
Many real cases are hybrids, such as native vegetation in New South Wales, protected in the public interest but mostly on private land.

definition.text: Stakeholder analysis identifies the different interest groups affected by how natural resources are used and conserved.

facts.text: Borrowed from business management, it is hard to apply because it is difficult to say who has a stake in a resource.
Its stages include identifying decision-makers and stakeholders, investigating their interests, and mapping conflicts, trade-offs and synergies.
A proposal to represent nature itself as a stakeholder has been rejected by many scholars as hard to put into practice.

title: Community-based natural resource management
article: Natural resource management#Community-based natural resource management

definition.text: Community-based natural resource management combines conservation goals with economic benefits for rural communities.

facts.text: It assumes locals are best placed to conserve resources, that people conserve only when benefits exceed costs, and that they protect what is tied to their quality of life.
It rests on subsidiarity, the principle of handling decisions at the most local level that can manage them.
Critics such as Tania Murray found that in upland Southeast Asia it could force communities to meet discriminatory conditions before gaining legal rights to resources.
Social capital and gender shape how it works in practice.

title: Integrated natural resource management
article: Natural resource management#Integrated natural resource management

definition.text: Integrated natural resource management manages resources systematically, balancing biophysical, political and economic aspects to meet both users' production goals and wider community goals.

facts.text: It focuses on sustainability and brings all stakeholders in from the planning stage to reduce later conflict.
It grew out of research on sustainable land use, participatory planning, integrated watershed management and adaptive management.

definition.text: The commons are the cultural and natural resources open to all members of a society, such as air, water and a habitable Earth.

facts.text: Commons can also mean resources that a group of users governs for themselves, through rules they create, rather than through the state or the market.
The word comes from the old English legal term for common land, and Garrett Hardin's 1968 article 'The Tragedy of the Commons' made it a general term for shared resources.
Before Hardin's article, academic titles mentioning 'the commons' or 'common property' were very rare.
In Mongolia, where herders moved collectively between pastures, grassland degradation was about 9%, against about 75% in Russia and 33% in China under state or household pastures.
Nepal handed forest control to communities from the late 1980s, giving locals a financial stake that encourages them to prevent overuse.
Globalization brings new pressures: resources like fish and timber are sold on world markets, making impacts harder for local communities to monitor.

definition.text: A set of rules Elinor Ostrom found in commons that are governed successfully, such as clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions.

facts.text: Early tragedy-of-the-commons work suggested all commons were doomed, but later economists found many successful ones, and Ostrom won the Nobel Prize for analysing them.
Ostrom found that farmers have run grazing commons in the Swiss Alps successfully for hundreds of years.
Her principles are clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, collective choice, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognised rights to organize and nested enterprises.
The principles work best when more than nine are used together.
The related 'comedy of the commons', coined by Carol M. Rose in 1986, describes users policing their own use to keep or improve a commons.

definition.text: Commoning treats the commons as an ongoing practice, the process of people coming together to manage shared resources, rather than as a thing.

facts.text: Some authors separate the shared resources, the community that governs them, and commoning, the act of managing them together.
In farming, commoning is the joint stewardship of shared land, and it matters to food systems in many communities worldwide.

definition.text: Urban commons are city resources managed by citizens themselves, valued by their use and upkeep costs rather than their market price.

facts.text: David Harvey argued that public spaces are not automatically commons; they become commons when citizens take political action there.
Urban commons work alongside the state and the market rather than replacing them.

definition.text: The global commons are shared resource areas, such as the high seas, the atmosphere, outer space and Antarctica, that lie beyond the political reach of any single nation.

facts.text: They hold common-pool resources: goods it is costly but not impossible to keep users out of, and which are used up by use, so they suffer congestion, overuse and degradation.
Their governance must avoid a worldwide tragedy of the commons, where shared resources are overexploited.
Global users are more varied than local ones, resources are less stable and harder to understand, and many are non-renewable on human time scales.
Carbon dioxide that drives climate change keeps doing so for at least a millennium after it enters the atmosphere.
International environmental agreements multiplied after the 1972 Stockholm conference, but they are often slow, settle for the lowest common denominator and lack enforcement.
The Montreal Protocol, in force from 1 January 1989, is widely seen as a highly successful model for managing the global commons.
The 1961 Antarctic Treaty sets Antarctica aside as a scientific preserve and bans military activity there.

title: Common ownership

definition.text: Common ownership means holding an organization's or community's assets as one undivided whole, not in the names of individual members.

facts.text: Forms of common ownership exist in every economic system.
Advocates separate collective ownership, shared by agreement among a set of members such as a producer cooperative, from common property open to all, such as a public park.
In capitalist economies it is practised by voluntary associations, non-profits and, implicitly, all public bodies.
Common ownership of the means of production is a central goal of socialist movements.

notes: The page's antitrust sense (investors owning shares in rival firms) is outside this course and is not drafted.

definition.text: In the incomplete-contracts approach of Oliver Hart and colleagues, ownership matters because the owner holds residual control rights: the say over an asset in any situation a contract does not cover.

facts.text: Owners have stronger incentives than non-owners to make investments tied to a relationship, so ownership can ease the hold-up problem.
A central result of this approach is that joint ownership, where each party can veto use of the asset, is suboptimal.
Later work shows joint ownership can be optimal when parties are unequally informed, in long-term relationships, or able to disclose know-how.

title: Customary land

definition.text: Customary land is land held and used under unwritten local custom rather than written, codified law.

facts.text: It is the tenure usually tied to indigenous communities, as opposed to statutory tenure mostly brought in during colonial times.
In many countries most land is customary, including 90% in Africa and 97% in Papua New Guinea.
The gap between formally recognized and customarily managed land is a major source of underdevelopment, conflict and environmental degradation.
The World Bank and others promote formal land titles, but opinion is divided on whether this always helps the poor.
Where several groups claim the same land, as often in Sub-Saharan Africa, formal titling can favour some and create tension.

contested_note: Sources say opinions are divided on whether formalizing customary land rights empowers the poor.

title: Enclosure

definition.text: Enclosure was the English practice of fencing off 'waste' or common land and taking it over, which stripped commoners of their traditional rights to use it.

facts.text: It merged scattered strips of land into large fields bounded by hedges, walls or fences, kept for the sole use of individual owners or their tenants.
Enclosure happened by owners making 'closes', by groups of proprietors enclosing whole parishes, and by acts of Parliament, the first in 1604.
Its stated aim was more efficient farming, but enclosed land also became much more valuable.
In Tudor England high wool profits led lords to turn common arable land into sheep pasture, evicting villagers.
Historians see enclosure riots as the leading form of social protest from the 1530s to the 1640s.
The movement probably peaked from 1760 to 1832, and surplus rural labour moved to towns to become industrial workers.
The Hammonds said enclosure ruined small farmers, cottagers and squatters, while Chambers and Mingay argued it brought more food, more cultivated land and more rural jobs.
Many Marxists see enclosure as 'primitive accumulation' that laid the ground for capitalism.

contested_note: Historians disagree on whether enclosure mainly impoverished rural people or raised food output and rural employment.

definition.text: Before enclosure, English common land lay under the manorial lord, with a manor made up of peasant tenants' holdings and the lord's own demesne farm.

facts.text: Tenants held rights such as pasture, pannage and estovers, and landless peasants often farmed narrow 'waste' strips nobody officially used.
Its end came with new methods such as the Norfolk four-course rotation, which raised crop and livestock yields by improving soil fertility and cutting fallow periods.

definition.text: Community forestry is a participatory approach, prominent since the 1970s, in which local communities take an active part in managing forests and deciding land use.

facts.text: The FAO defines it as any situation that closely involves local people in forestry.
It manages forests both for income from timber and non-timber products and for ecosystem services such as watershed protection and carbon storage.
It is seen as one of the most promising ways to combine forest conservation with rural development and poverty reduction.
Nepal's democratically run Forest User Groups have regenerated forests, with some regions seeing a 37% rise in forest cover.
Secure land tenure decides whether communities can invest in sustainable practices; unclear boundaries, elite capture and weak enforcement threaten projects.
Certification and carbon credits open global markets, but high certification costs remain a barrier for smallholders.
There is no single blueprint, because regional social, economic and environmental conditions differ.

definition.text: The IAD framework is Elinor Ostrom's theoretical tool for studying how people, called actors, interact with common-pool resources.

facts.text: Common-pool resources are rivalrous, since one person's use reduces others', and non-excludable, since keeping people out is impractical; forests and pastures are examples.
Built on rational choice assumptions, it explains outcomes by documenting governance structures, actors' positions and formal and informal rules.
It breaks complex collective action problems into smaller 'action arenas'.
Institutions are studied through seven rule types: position, boundary, choice, aggregation, information, pay-off and scope.

title: International Association for the Study of the Commons
article: International Association for the Study of the Commons

definition.text: A non-profit association founded in 1989 to advance understanding of institutions for managing resources held or used in common.

facts.text: It publishes the open-access International Journal of the Commons and holds biennial global conferences.
Elinor Ostrom was a founding member and its first president.

title: Governing the Commons

definition.text: Governing the Commons (1990) is Elinor Ostrom's best-known book, showing that communities worldwide have managed shared resources successfully through local rules.

facts.text: It drew on irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines, mountain villages in Switzerland and Japan, and fisheries in Nova Scotia and Indonesia.
In it Ostrom set out eight design principles found in long-lasting common-pool resource institutions.
It argues that self-interest need not always cause degradation and can lead people to care for common property resources.

notes: Phrase concept (a book) with no page of its own; may fold into Ostrom's design principles or the Ostrom founder entry.

title: Joint Forest Management

definition.text: Joint Forest Management is India's term for partnerships in which state forest departments and local communities share forest protection and development.

facts.text: It is set out in India's National Forest Policy of 1988 and guidelines of 1990, and began in Odisha in 1988.
With Nepal's Forest User Groups, it was an early response to failing centralized forest policy.

notes: Phrase-dossier concept that does have a crawled page; country-specific, kept Minor as a leading example of co-management.
